name: Radiendocrinator

card.summary: A 1930s radium-containing device marketed to be worn against the skin over the endocrine glands, promoted for general vitality and rejuvenation.
card.note: Radioactive; its maker's related radium products are associated with fatal radiation illness.

quick.overview:
The Radiendocrinator was a small cased radioactive source invented around 1930 by William J. A. Bailey, a patent-medicine salesman, and designed to be worn against the skin. Radium products of the era were sold as tonics for vigor and youthfulness, which is the appearance-related promise attached to such devices.

Publicly available information about the device itself is limited. The better-documented part of the story is Bailey's related product Radithor, a radium-water drink, and the death of one of its users, Eben Byers, in 1932.
quick.how: As described, the device was worn against the skin, placed on the body near the glands it was said to stimulate. Specific marketing claims, radium content and price are not documented in the references available here.
quick.risks: The device contained a radioactive source. Bailey himself died of bladder cancer in 1949, and his exhumed body was reported to be ravaged by radiation. Radium consumer products of this type are no longer marketed.

lead: The Radiendocrinator was a cased radioactive source intended to be worn against the skin, invented by William J. A. Bailey around 1930 [1].

Bailey was a Boston-born patent medicine inventor and salesman who falsely claimed to be a doctor. His Associated Radium Chemists sold radium tablets and other products from 1922, and his best-known product, Radithor, consisted of radium salts in water that he said stimulated the endocrine system [1].

As with other radium tonics, the underlying promise was revitalization of the body, which is how such devices were connected to a better-looking, more youthful self. Bailey's company was repeatedly investigated by the Federal Trade Commission [1].

chain: Radium source worn against the skin over glands
Claimed stimulation of the endocrine system
angle.text: Promoters presented radium devices as a way to stimulate the glands and restore vigor. No studies of the Radiendocrinator are known; its place in history is as an example of radioactive consumer products.

paras: Accounts describe the Radiendocrinator as a cased radioactive source meant to be worn against the skin. Details such as exact placement, radium quantity and price are not given in the sources consulted, and the name suggests glands of the endocrine system as the intended target [1].

Bailey (1884-1949) attended Boston Latin School and was accepted to Harvard but did not graduate. In 1918 he began claiming that radium in drinking water could treat conditions ranging from mental illness to asthma, and by 1922 his company sold several radium products [1].

Eben Byers, a socialite and athlete, died in 1932 of radiation-induced cancer after drinking about 1,400 bottles of Radithor, an event associated with the decline of radium patent medicines [1]. Bailey's Radium Laboratories in East Orange, New Jersey, was repeatedly investigated by the FTC, and Bailey died of bladder cancer in 1949 [1].

timeline.event: Bailey's company sells radium products including tablets [1].
Eben Byers dies after heavy Radithor consumption [1].
